title: Chapter 116: OCD
html:
Men Nan stubbornly refused to sleep, remaining in the middle of the room with his head held at that unnatural angle, as though trying to wrench it free of his neck.

“It looks as if something is pressing down on his head.” Afraid of agitating Men Nan, Chen Ge lowered his voice. “Not psychological pressure—something physically real.”

Doctor Gao discreetly waved him off and stayed beside Men Nan. He took out his phone and began typing a message. When he offered no spoken reply, Chen Ge moved away to inspect the apartment.

The place was just over thirty square meters, but it had everything: a bedroom, living room, and a standalone bathroom.

It looks like an ordinary rental apartment.

Chen Ge searched every corner and found nowhere large enough to conceal a body. He left the living room and pushed open the wooden bathroom door. To his surprise, a half-length mirror hung on the wall directly opposite the entrance.

The mirror faces the door?

Ever since his first Nightmare Mission, Chen Ge had been wary of mirrors. He approached slowly and studied his reflection. People rarely place a mirror directly across from a door. Something about this feels wrong.

The glass was spotless, as though someone cleaned it constantly. Beneath it stood a sink—the setting from Men Nan’s nightmare.

Chen Ge assumed the position Men Nan had described. He bent almost ninety-five degrees at the waist until his head barely reached the faucet. From here, I can see into the living room. Everything in his dream could have happened exactly as he described.

If the angle had blocked his view of the living room, Chen Ge might have felt reassured; that would have suggested Men Nan’s experience was only a dream.

Instead, his test proved that every detail could have occurred in reality. With his head beneath the faucet, the room turned upside down around him.

Men Nan said the man comes closer each time. Why prolong the torment instead of attacking him at once? Is there some history between them?

As Chen Ge considered the question, something cold struck the back of his neck. He straightened at once and touched the spot.

A drop of water? Where did it come from?He looked up, but the ceiling was dry. The water seemed to have appeared from nowhere.

Could it have come from the mirror?He imagined his reflection climbing out to strangle him as he washed his hair.

The black phone called this Trial Mission A Room of Three. The name itself must be a clue.Chen Ge stared at his reflection as an idea took shape. There are three “people” in this room. Men Nan is one, and the man from his dream is another. Who is the third? Could it be hiding inside the mirror?

Bracing both hands on the sink, Chen Ge glanced around and spotted two empty shampoo bottles in the bathroom trash can.

Men Nan hasn’t lived here long, yet he has already emptied two bottles? If he washes his hair only in dreams, why is the real shampoo disappearing? Does he sleepwalk and wash it during the night?After some thought, Chen Ge dismissed the possibility. Doctor Gao had once taken Men Nan into his own home, yet the nightmares had continued.

Then he must be doing it while awake, which is even stranger. Why use so much shampoo?

Even an exceptionally fastidious person might wash their hair only twice a day, but Men Nan had drained two bottles in a short time. Then Chen Ge noticed a third bottle on the sink, already half empty.

What would make someone wash their hair so compulsively? Dandruff? A skin condition? Or is he trying to scrub something away?Chen Ge leaned against the wall and thought. He argued with his classmates over the animals on a curtain and the number of sesame seeds on a cracker. His behavior does sound like severe OCD.

When people with OCD noticed something out of place, they often felt compelled to correct it; if they could not, the discomfort could become overwhelming. Chen Ge suspected Men Nan’s obsessive hair washing stemmed from the same impulse.

Only Men Nan can explain it. He must be hiding something important from Doctor Gao.

Chen Ge’s phone suddenly vibrated. To his surprise, the message was from Doctor Gao.

“Men Nan’s family situation is more complicated than I thought. When I told them about his condition, they accepted it far too calmly. They promised to cover his medical expenses, but none of them plans to visit him in Jiujiang. I didn’t want Men Nan to overhear, so I’m telling you by phone.”

“Their son is ill, and his parents don’t even want to see him?”

“I didn’t expect it either. His friends all believed he came from a happy family. I checked his social media, and he has shared countless posts about how much he loves them.” Men Nan had carefully constructed the image of a warm, loving home and of himself as an educated, cheerful, diligent young man. In the end, it was only a facade.

After reading the message, Chen Ge texted Doctor Gao about the shampoo. A reply arrived soon afterward.

“OCD is commonly divided into four categories: checking, rumination, contamination, and symmetry and order. From what I’ve observed, Men Nan’s symptoms don’t fit neatly into any of them. His compulsive hair washing appears to satisfy a separate need.

“I believe Men Nan may instead be suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. Earthquake survivors, for example, can remain hypervigilant long after the tremors stop. They struggle to move beyond the trauma because their minds keep warning them that another quake could strike at any moment.

“Men Nan shows similar signs. He is constantly on guard, and his eyes keep darting around as though searching for danger. The hair washing may be a form of self-protection.”
